items.note: The setup is given in full: "Let $\zeta=e^{\pi i/r}$, so $\zeta^r=-1$. Define $\Theta:\mathbb C[x_d]/(x_d^r-1)\to\mathcal R_r$ by $x_d\mapsto\zeta y$", and $\mathcal R_r=\mathbb C[y]/(y^r+1)$ is defined in the opening paragraph, as in paper lines 4302-4307.

The page gives well-definedness from "$(\zeta y)^r=(-1)(-1)=1$" (with $\zeta^r=-1$ shown just before), gets diagonality from "$\Theta(x_d^k)=\zeta^k y^k$", concludes isomorphism with inverse $\zeta^{-k}$, and gets sup-norm preservation from "$|\zeta^{\pm k}|=1$". This matches paper lines 4308-4312 and supplies the norm reason the paper leaves implicit.

The page writes $k+l=j+hr$ with $h\in\{0,1\}$. It explains that the twist contributes $\zeta^{k+l}$ and negacyclic reduction contributes $(-1)^h$, displays $\zeta^{k+l}(-1)^h=\zeta^j(\zeta^r)^h(-1)^h=\zeta^j$, and concludes that untwisting by $\zeta^{-j}$ recovers the cyclic coefficient, as in paper lines 4313-4320. The worked $r=2$ example (constant term $f_0g_0+f_1g_1$, $y$-coefficient $i(f_0g_1+f_1g_0)$) is correct.

The page defines $M=T/r$, $\iota$ and $D_\pm$, notes that $\iota D_+$ applies $\Theta$ linewise with inverse $D_-\iota^{-1}$, says $\mathcal M_r$ convolves the first $d-1$ axes dividing by $T$, and gives the identity $=f*g/T$, following paper lines 4321-4347. The contraction is shown explicitly: $\mathcal M_r$ averages $rM$ signed products (paper 3378-3387), and the isometries give $\|\mathcal M_{\mathbb C}(f,g)\|\le\|f\|\|g\|$. The equality itself is linked to the ring isomorphism only implicitly, through the opening remark that convolution along the last axis is multiplication in $\mathbb C[x_d]/(x_d^r-1)$. That is about as much as the paper's own "Consequently".
